explanations.explanation: Step out to the country and it's the sword. Step into the city and it's famine. Those are the two sights the word gives, side by side. I think this verse is heavy, so I'll let it be heavy.
That's a calm picture, friend, but this word doesn't paint it. The city shows those ravaged by famine. Nobody's gathered anywhere cozy in this verse. It's a hard one, so I'll just say it plainly.

I love a hopeful answer, and I'm sorry this verse doesn't have one. Rebuilding walls isn't what it says. What Jeremiah sees in the city is those ravaged by famine. It's a heavy verse, so we'll carry it together.
Yes, friend. The word names both prophet and priest, and both travel to a land they do not know. The verse says it about the two of them together. I think that makes it hit even harder.

This one is actually true. The word says that both prophet and priest travel to a land they do not know. They're both named, so neither gets left out. It's a tough line to read twice, and that's okay.

Peace is the word. They hoped for peace, and the prayer says no good has come. They also hoped for a time of healing. What showed up was terror. That's a lot of hoping with nothing to show for it, friend.

Victory is a big, shiny word, but the prayer doesn't ask for a win. It says they hoped for peace. Nobody's talking about a trophy here, just a quiet place to breathe. I think that's the more honest wish anyway.

Nobody in this prayer is counting coins, friend. They say they hoped for peace, and then they hoped for a time of healing. Hoping for peace and healing is a very different list from hoping for riches. Plain, tired hope, and it still came up empty.

Not quite, friend. The prayer says, “We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, the guilt of our fathers; indeed, we have sinned against You.” The fathers get named, but so do the ones praying. They don't hand the whole load to somebody else.

You've got it. The prayer does mention “…the guilt of our fathers…” but it doesn't stop there. Right alongside it comes, “indeed, we have sinned against You.” They own it for themselves, and that's not easy to do.

Right on. The prayer says, “Remember Your covenant with us; do not break it.” Just before this they say they have sinned against Him, so they're not leaning on a record of their own. They're pointing at the covenant the LORD made with them. That's a solid place to stand when everything else is shaky.

Good guess, but this prayer doesn't brag about a record. Just before this they say they have sinned against Him. So they don't ask Him to count their years of worship. They ask Him to remember His covenant with them.

The fathers do show up in this prayer, but only as guilt, in verse 20. The ask here isn't about anything they offered. It's “Remember Your covenant with us; do not break it.” The covenant is what they lean on.
That's the answer. The prayer asks, “Is this not by You, O LORD our God?” Then it says, “So we put our hope in You…” When the sky is dry, they know exactly who to look to.

The prayer does ask, “Do the skies alone send showers?” But it asks it as a question, and it doesn't leave it hanging. Right after, it says, “Is this not by You, O LORD our God?” The skies don't get the credit.

The prayer asks, “Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain?” and it calls them worthless in the same breath. Asking an idol for rain is like yelling at an empty cookie jar for a fresh batch. The prayer points to the LORD our God instead.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and Samuel, a prophet (1 Samuel 3:20). Those are two mighty names, and the LORD says that even if they stood before Him, His heart would not go out to this people. I think that tells us how heavy this moment is.

Elijah, a prophet, and Elisha, who was anointed to take his place (1 Kings 19:16). Good names, but the LORD doesn't say them here. In this verse He names Moses and Samuel. Still, mixing up two prophets is understandable, friend.
Abraham, and his son Isaac (Genesis 21:3). Big names, no doubt, but they aren't the ones the LORD names in this verse. He says Moses and Samuel. Keep going, friend, you're doing fine.
That's not what the LORD says, friend. When they ask where to go, Jeremiah is to tell them, “Those destined for death, to death…” No safe place gets pointed out. I think this one stings.

Right. The answer Jeremiah is given for them starts, “Those destined for death, to death…” It's four different destinations, and not one of them is a safe place. It's a hard line, and you read it well.

Yes, Manasseh, king of Judah and Hezekiah's son. The LORD says He will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem. The text puts his name right there in verse 4. Good eye, friend.

Ahaz, another king of Judah and the son of Jotham (2 Kings 16:1). He's a real king, but he's not the one named here. The LORD names Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Kings of Judah were plentiful, friend, and I'd have to squint at that list too.

Jehoram, a king of Judah and the son of Jehoshaphat (2 Kings 8:16). Another real king, but the LORD doesn't name him in this verse. The one named is Manasseh son of Hezekiah. That's a lot of long names to keep straight.
Yes. The LORD says, “You have forsaken Me…” and then, “You have turned your back.” It's two plain lines, and He says them straight to Jerusalem. That's hard to hear, and you read it right.

The text says it the other way, friend. The LORD tells Jerusalem, “You have forsaken Me…” and right after that, “You have turned your back.” It's two plain lines, no mystery in them. A hard thing to read, so I'm glad you stuck with it.

Compassion is the word. The LORD says, “I am weary of showing compassion.” That's a sobering line, and it sits right next to His stretching out His hand against them. I think it's okay to stay quiet over it for a moment.
I can see why anger comes to mind, but that's not the word here. The LORD says, “I am weary of showing compassion.” Compassion is what He says He is weary of showing. That's a heavy one.
Strength isn't the word, friend. The LORD says, “I am weary of showing compassion.” Compassion is the word at the end of that line. It's a sober thing to read.

explanations.answer: Those who have not turned from their ways
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says He will bereave and destroy “…My people who have not turned from their ways.” It's about who hasn't turned, and not about where anyone lives. Notice that He still calls them His people.

explanations.answer: Those who live in the far villages
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't sort anyone by where they live. It says the LORD will bereave and destroy “…My people who have not turned from their ways.” No villages get named. The line is about the ones who haven't turned.

explanations.answer: Those who fled from Jerusalem first
explanations.explanation: Nobody's order of leaving comes up in this verse. The LORD says He will bereave and destroy “…My people who have not turned from their ways.” That's the group He names. Fleeing first isn't part of it, friend.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says, “I will make their widows more numerous than the sand of the sea.” That's a number too big to count, not one you could count on a hand. It's a heavy verse, so I'll say that once and leave it there.

Right. The LORD says, “I will make their widows more numerous than the sand of the sea.” Nobody could count that on one hand, or on a thousand hands. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to feel that.

Yes. The text says, “she will be disgraced and humiliated.” That's said of the mother of seven, who will grow faint, breathe her last breath, and whose sun will set while it is still day. This is one of the heaviest lines in the passage, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.

Poverty isn't in this verse, friend. The text says the mother of seven grows faint and breathes her last breath. Then it says, “she will be disgraced and humiliated.” That's a heavy line, and it's the one the text gives.

A long sickness isn't what the verse says. It says the mother of seven will grow faint and breathe her last breath, and her sun will set while it is still day. Then it says, “she will be disgraced and humiliated.” Hard words, so I'll go gently here.
